description: We are a team passionate about technology, software development, and space exploration. We aim to build innovative applications that solve real-world problems while learning and collaborating.
summary: MoonWindow shows whether a lander at the lunar south pole will have sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for radio, when that changes, and for how long. Near the pole the Sun and Earth skim the horizon, so a ridge a few degrees high decides the answer. MoonWindow therefore traces the real horizon from NASA LRO LOLA terrain instead of assuming flat ground. It checks every site against NASA’s Artemis III landing rules, finds the best landing spot inside each of NASA’s 9 Artemis III candidate regions, and plans landing dates. Its results are validated against NASA JPL Horizons, NASA Goddard polar illumination maps, LRO camera images, and the 12° slope NASA estimated where IM-1 Odysseus tipped over (MoonWindow computes 11.6°).
details:
What it does: pick any landing site (9 real missions, NASA’s 9 Artemis III candidate regions, or any coordinates) and any date. MoonWindow shows a 3D Moon, a 360° view of the sky from the site with the real skyline, where the Sun and Earth are now, and countdowns to the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset. It also gives 30-day timelines of sunlight, Earth visibility and both together, solar energy for a given panel size, and the dates when both stay up long enough for a mission. Up to 3 scenarios can be compared side by side, for example the same site before and after a launch slip.

How it works: Sun and Earth positions come from Astronomy Engine with the IAU lunar orientation model, checked against NASA JPL Horizons (72 comparisons, largest difference 0.003°). For each site we trace the terrain outward 400 km in 720 directions on NASA LOLA elevation maps (80 m and 240 m) and record the highest terrain angle seen from 2 m above the ground, the same method used for NASA’s polar illumination maps. Any other point south of 77°S gets its skyline computed in the browser from compressed LOLA grids.

Validation: against NASA Goddard’s polar maps at 96 points, the sunlight error is 2.8 percentage points, versus 32.9 for flat ground. Against about 25,000 patches in LRO camera frames, light and dark are classified correctly 96.8% of the time (flat ground: 77.3%). Of the 7-day landing windows our planner approved, camera images contradicted none of 34; with flat ground they contradicted 150 of 217.

Artemis III: each NASA region is about 15 × 15 km, and a lander needs a 100 m spot. For each region we tested 7,845 points against NASA’s rules (slope under 10°, Earth in view at least 25% of the year) and picked the sunniest. At Slater Plain, the region’s coordinate gets 4% sunlight a year; the best spot 4.8 km away gets 66% and passes all 4 rules.

Why it matters: power and communication windows drive lander design, landing dates and site choice. Flat-ground estimates can be wrong by 30 percentage points at the pole.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML/CSS and WebGL in a single offline web page; Python and Node.js for data processing. Open source on GitHub: https://github.com/MykolaBohomaz/Nasa-Space-Apps-Lunar-Landing-Site-Navigator
